drivingQuestion: What underlies the tannaitic dispute whether a runaway slave-nazirite may drink wine?
outcomeNote: the Shmuel-based ground is rejected; the dispute is about the slave's return incentive

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ לֵימָא בְּדִשְׁמוּאֵל קָמִיפַּלְגִי, דְּאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הַמַּפְקִיר עַבְדּוֹ יָצָא לְחֵירוּת, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ גֵּט שִׁיחְרוּר.
segments.en: «GEMARA:» The Gemara suggests: «Shall we say» that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei «disagree with regard to» the following statement «of Shmuel? As Shmuel said:» With regard to one «who renounces ownership of his slave,» the slave «is emancipated, and he does not require a bill of manumission.» This halakha indicates that if a slave is free in practice, he no longer requires a bill of manumission but is automatically considered a freeman.

segments.he: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אִית לֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי לֵית לֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: If so, should one say that «Rabbi Meir is of» the opinion that the ruling is in accordance with the opinion «of Shmuel,» and therefore the slave is obligated in naziriteship as soon as he runs away, like any other freed slave, and «Rabbi Yosei is of» the opinion that the ruling is «not» in accordance with the opinion «of Shmuel?»

segments.he: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל. אֶלָּא: מַאן דְּאָמַר יִשְׁתֶּה, סָבַר: סוֹף סוֹף מִיהְדָּר הָדַר וְאָתֵי גַּבֵּיהּ, לִישְׁתֵּי חַמְרָא כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לִיכְחוֹשׁ. וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר לֹא יִשְׁתֶּה, סָבַר: לֶיהֱוֵי לֵיהּ צַעְרָא כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיהְדַּר גַּבֵּיהּ.
segments.en: The Gemara rejects this suggestion: «No,» it is possible «that everyone is of» the opinion that the ruling is in accordance with the opinion «of Shmuel. Rather,» the mishna is referring to a case where the master refused to declare the runaway ownerless, and was intent on recovering him. Consequently, the slave is not in fact a freeman at all, and the tanna’im disagree with regard to the following: Rabbi Yosei, «the one who says» that «he may drink» wine, «maintains» that the slave «will ultimately return and come back to» his master, and therefore it is preferable for him «to drink wine so that he should not be weakened» by the time he returns. «And according to» Rabbi Meir, «the one who says» that «he may not drink» wine, he «maintains» that it is better that the slave «should suffer» by being deprived of wine, «so that he will return to» his master, as the desire to drink wine will spur him to return.
